6. The Singing-Match: Damoetas and Daphnis
Damoetas and Daphnis the cowherd once drove their herd
together into one place, Aratus; and one of them
was red-haired, the other half-bearded; and sitting both by a spring
at midday in the summer, they sang in this way.
Daphnis began first, for it was he who first challenged.
Galatea pelts your flock, Polyphemus,
with apples, calling you a laggard in love, a goatherd;
and you do not even look at her, poor wretch, poor wretch, but sit
piping sweetly. Look, again she pelts the dog,
which follows as guardian of your sheep; and it barks,
gazing toward the sea, and the fair waves show it
softly plashing as it runs along the shore.
Take care, lest she leap upon the girl's legs
as she comes from the sea, and tear her lovely skin.
But she even from there coquets with you, light
as the dry thistledown when the fair summer parches it;
and she flees the one who loves her, and pursues the one who does not,
and moves her last counter on the line; for to a lover,
Polyphemus, things not fair often appear fair.
After him Damoetas struck up and sang as follows.
I saw her, by Pan, when she was pelting the flock,
and she did not escape my notice, no, by this one sweet eye of mine, with which I shall see
to the end; but as for the seer Telemus, who speaks ill words,
let him bear his ill words home, to keep them for his children.
Yet I myself, to tease her in turn, do not look at her,
but say I have some other woman; and she, hearing this,
grows jealous of me, by the Healer, and pines away, and from the sea
she peers out in a frenzy at the caves and at the flocks.
And I hissed the dog to bark at her; for when I loved her,
it would whimper, laying its muzzle against her flank.
Seeing me do this often, perhaps she will send
a messenger. But I will bar my doors, until she swears
to spread a fair bed for me herself upon this island.
For indeed I am not so ill to look at as they say.
The other day I gazed into the sea, when it was calm,
and fair my beard, and fair my one eye seemed,
so far as I could judge, and the gleam of my teeth
showed whiter than the marble of Paros.
And, lest I be bewitched, I spat three times into my bosom;
for so the old woman Cotyttaris taught me.
Having said so much, Damoetas kissed Daphnis,
and the one gave him a pipe, the other a fine flute.
Damoetas played the flute, and Daphnis the cowherd piped,
and at once the heifers danced upon the soft grass.
But neither was the victor, for they came out unbeaten.

7. The Harvest-Home
There was a time when Eucritus and I were walking from the city
toward the Hales, and a third with us was Amyntas;
for to Demeter, Phrasidamus and Antigenes were keeping
the harvest-feast, two sons of Lycopeus, the best of any noble line
descended from above, from Clytia and from Chalcon himself,
who brought the spring Burina forth at the touch of his foot,
setting his knee firmly against the rock; and beside it
poplars and elms wove a shady grove,
roofed over and leafy with their green foliage.
We had not yet finished half the road, nor had the tomb
of Brasilas come into our sight, when by the favor of the Muses
we met a good wayfarer, a man of Cydonia,
Lycidas by name, a goatherd, nor could anyone
mistake him at a glance, for he looked a goatherd through and through.
For from a shaggy, rough-haired he-goat he had
a tawny skin upon his shoulders, smelling of fresh rennet,
and about his breast an old cloak was girt
with a broad belt, and in his right hand he held
a crooked club of wild olive. And gently, with a grin
and a smiling eye, he spoke to me, and laughter clung to his lip:
Simichidas, where are you dragging your feet at noon,
when even the lizard sleeps in the dry-stone walls,
and the crested larks of the tombs do not roam abroad?
Are you hurrying to a feast you were bidden to? Or do you leap
to some townsman's wine-press? For as you go, every
stone strikes ringing against your boots and sings.
And I answered him: Dear Lycidas, all men say
you are by far the best of pipers among the herdsmen
and among the reapers. This greatly warms my heart;
and yet in my own mind I hope to be your match.
This journey is to a harvest-feast; for some comrades
are making a banquet to fair-robed Demeter,
offering the first-fruits of their wealth; for with a rich measure
the goddess has filled their threshing-floor with abundant barley.
But come now—the road is common to us, and common too the dawn—
let us make our herdsman's songs; perhaps one will profit the other.
For I too am a clear-voiced mouth of the Muses, and all men call me
the best of singers; but I am not quick to believe,
no, by Earth; for in my own judgment I do not yet outsing
either the noble Sicelidas of Samos or Philitas,
but contend like a frog against the crickets.
So I spoke, on purpose; and the goatherd, with a sweet laugh,
said: I give you this club as a gift, because you are
a sapling shaped by Zeus, all true.
For I greatly hate the builder who tries
to raise a house as high as the peak of Oromedon the mountain,
and those cocks of the Muses who, crowing in rivalry
against the bard of Chios, toil all in vain.
But come, let us quickly begin the herdsman's song,
Simichidas; and I—see, friend, whether you like
this little song that I worked at on the hill the other day.
Lycidas
A fair voyage to Mitylene shall Ageanax have,
both when the south wind drives the wet waves before the Kids at evening,
and when Orion sets his feet upon the ocean,
if only he rescues Lycidas, who is scorched by Aphrodite;
for hot love for him consumes me.
And the halcyons shall calm the waves and the sea
and the south wind and the east, that stirs the seaweed in the deeps;
the halcyons, of all birds dearest to the gray Nereids,
and to all whose prey is gathered from the sea.
For Ageanax, who seeks a voyage to Mitylene,
may all be seasonable, and may he reach a safe harbor.
And I, on that day, with anise or roses
or with a wreath of white violets about my head,
will draw the Ptelean wine from the bowl,
lying beside the fire, while someone roasts a bean in the embers.
And the couch will be heaped a cubit deep
with fleabane and asphodel and curling celery.
And I will drink at ease, remembering Ageanax,
draining the very cups, pressing my lip to the dregs.
Two shepherds will play the flute for me, one from Acharnae,
one from Lycope; and Tityrus close by will sing
how once Daphnis the cowherd loved Xenea,
and how the mountain grieved about him, and how the oaks lamented him,
those that grow along the banks of the river Himeras,
while he melted like snow under high Haemus
or Athos or Rhodope or the far Caucasus.
And he will sing how once the wide chest received the goatherd,
still living, through the wicked malice of his lord,
and how the snub-nosed bees, coming from the meadow,
fed him in the sweet cedar-chest with soft flowers,
because the Muse poured sweet nectar over his mouth.
O blessed Comatas, these are the joys you knew;
you too were shut into the chest, and you, fed on the bees'
honeycomb, lived out the spring of the year.
Would that you had been counted among the living in my day,
that I might have pastured your fair goats upon the hills,
listening to your voice, while you under the oaks or the pines
lay piping sweetly, godlike Comatas.
When he had said so much he ceased; and after him in turn
I too spoke thus: Dear Lycidas, many other
fair things have the Nymphs taught me too, as I herded on the hills,
songs that perhaps even rumor has carried to the throne of Zeus;
but this is the best by far of all, with which I will begin
to honor you; only listen, since you are dear to the Muses.
Simichidas
The Loves have sneezed for Simichidas; for the poor wretch
loves Myrto as much as goats love the spring.
But Aratus, dearest of all to that man,
keeps in his heart a longing for a boy. Aristis knows it,
a good man, a great and excellent man, whom not even Phoebus himself
would grudge to sing with his lyre beside the tripods,
how Aratus from a boy has been burned to the bone with love.
For him, Pan, you who have the lovely plain of Homole for your portion,
set the boy unbidden in his dear hands,
whether it is soft Philinus or some other.
And if you do this, dear Pan, then may no Arcadian boys
scourge your sides and shoulders with squills
when there is scant meat at hand;
but if you nod the other way, then may you scratch and bite
yourself all over with your nails, and sleep among the nettles,
and may you be in the mountains of the Edonians at midwinter,
turned toward the river Hebrus, close to the Bear,
and in summer pasture among the farthest Ethiopians
under the rock of the Blemyes, whence the Nile is seen no more.
But you Loves, leaving the sweet stream of Hyetis and Byblis,
and Oecus, the steep seat of golden Dione,
you who are like to ruddy apples,
strike for me with your bows the lovely Philinus,
strike him, since the wretch has no pity on my friend the stranger.
And indeed he is now more overripe than a pear, and the women
say, Alas, Philinus, your fair bloom is dropping away.
Let us no longer keep watch at his doors, Aratus,
nor wear out our feet; but let the cock at dawn,
crowing, give some other man over to bitter numbness,
and let one man only, good Molon, be throttled at that wrestling-school,
while ease be our care, and an old woman be at hand,
who, spitting, may ward off all that is unlovely.
So much I said; and he, with a sweet laugh
as before, gave me the throwing-stick to be a gift of friendship from the Muses.
And he, turning aside to the left, took the road
to Pyxa; while Eucritus and I, and the fair Amyntichus,
turning to the house of Phrasidamus, lay down
among deep beds of sweet rushes,
rejoicing in the newly stripped vine-leaves.
Many poplars and elms waved above
over our heads; and close by, the holy water
trickled murmuring from the cave of the Nymphs.
In the shady boughs the sun-burnt cicadas
kept their chattering toil; and far off the tree-frog
cried among the thick thorns of the brambles.
The larks and goldfinches sang, the turtle-dove moaned,
and the tawny bees flitted about the springs.
All breathed of rich summer, all breathed of harvest-time.
Pears at our feet, and apples by our sides
rolled in abundance; and the boughs hung down to the ground
weighted with sloes;
and the four-year-old seal was loosed from the wine-jars' mouths.
You Nymphs of Castalia, who hold the peak of Parnassus,
was it ever such a bowl as this that old Chiron
set up for Heracles in the rocky cave of Pholus?
Was it such nectar that prompted that shepherd by the Anapus,
mighty Polyphemus, who hurled mountains at ships,
to dance about the steadings on his feet,
as the draught you then mingled for us, you Nymphs,
beside the altar of Demeter of the threshing-floor? Upon her heap
may I once again plant the great winnowing-fan,
while she smiles, holding sheaves and poppies in both her hands.

8. The Singing-Match: Daphnis and Menalcas
With the graceful Daphnis, as he herded his cattle,
Menalcas met, pasturing his sheep, they say, on the long hills.
Both of them were red-haired, both still beardless,
both skilled in piping, both in singing.
And Menalcas, looking at Daphnis, was the first to speak:
Daphnis, guardian of the lowing cattle, will you sing against me?
I say I will beat you, singing as long as I choose.
And Daphnis answered him with these words:
Menalcas, shepherd of the woolly sheep, you piper,
you will never beat me, however you may strain at singing.
Menalcas
Then do you care to put it to the test? Do you care to set up a prize?
Daphnis
I care to put it to the test; I care to set up a prize.
Menalcas
And what shall we stake that would be worthy of us?
Daphnis
I will stake a calf; do you stake a lamb as big as its mother.
Menalcas
I will never stake a lamb, for my father is harsh,
and my mother too, and they count all the sheep at evening.
Daphnis
But what then will you stake? What more shall the winner have?
Menalcas
A pipe that I made, a fair one of nine reeds,
set with white wax, even below and even above—
this I will stake; but I will not stake my father's goods.
Daphnis
Why, I too have a pipe of nine reeds,
set with white wax, even below and even above.
I fitted it together the other day; and I still feel a pain
in this finger, where a reed split and cut me.
Menalcas
But who shall judge between us? Who shall hear us?
Daphnis
What if we call that goatherd over here,
the one at whose kids the white-spotted dog is barking?
So the boys shouted, and the goatherd came to listen.
The boys sang, and the goatherd was willing to judge.
And first, having drawn the lot, the loud-voiced Menalcas sang,
then Daphnis took up the answering song.
Menalcas
You glens and rivers, race divine, if ever Menalcas
the piper sang you a song you loved,
graze his ewe-lambs with a good will; and if ever Daphnis
come with his heifers, may he have no less.
Daphnis
You springs and pastures, sweet growth, if Daphnis
makes music like the nightingales,
fatten this herd of mine; and if Menalcas
brings any here, may he too feed all in plenty, and rejoice.
Menalcas
Here are the ewes, here the goats that bear twins, here the bees
fill their hives, and here the oaks grow taller,
here the fair Milon sets his feet; but if he goes away,
then dry are both the shepherd and the pastures there.
Daphnis
Spring everywhere, everywhere the meadows, everywhere with milk
the udders swell, and the young are reared,
wherever the fair girl walks; but if she goes away,
then withered are both the cowherd and his cattle.
Menalcas
O he-goat, husband of the white she-goats, O depth of the woodland
without end—(O snub-nosed kids, come here to the water)—
for there he is; go, you stub-horned one, and say: Milon,
even Proteus, though a god, pastured his seals.
Daphnis
May I not have the land of Pelops, nor talents of gold
to possess, nor to outrun the winds;
but under this rock will I sing, holding you in my arms,
watching the flocks graze together, toward the Sicilian sea.
Daphnis
For the trees winter is a dread evil, for the waters drought,
for the birds the snare, for the wild beasts the net,
for a man the longing for a tender maiden. O father, O Zeus,
I am not the only one to have loved; you too love women.
So the boys sang in answering strains;
and Menalcas led off the last song in this way.
Spare my kids, wolf, spare my mothers,
and do me no wrong, though I am small and tend so many.
O Lampurus, my dog, are you held by so deep a sleep?
You should not sleep deeply when you herd with a boy.
And you, my ewes, do not be slow to feed your fill on the soft
grass; you will not tire, for it will grow again.
Hsst, graze, graze, and fill your udders, all of you,
that the lambs may have part, and part I may lay by in the baskets.
Then Daphnis in his turn struck up clear-voiced to sing:
And me too, the other day, a girl with meeting brows, looking from the cave
as I drove my heifers past, called fair, fair;
but I gave her no answer back, not even a bitter one,
but looking down I went on my own way.
Sweet is the heifer's voice, sweet her breath;
and sweet in summer to lie in the open air by running water.
For the oak the acorns are an ornament, for the apple-tree the apples,
for the cow the calf, for the cowherd the cattle themselves.
So the boys sang, and the goatherd spoke thus:
Sweet is your mouth, Daphnis, and lovely your voice.
Better to hear you singing than to lick honey.
Take the pipes; for you have won in the singing.
And if you are willing to teach me too, who herd goats beside you,
I will give you that hornless goat as your teaching-fee,
who always fills the pail above the brim.
As the boy rejoiced and leaped and clapped his hands,
having won, so might a fawn leap to its mother;
and as the other smoldered and was overturned in his heart with grief,
so might a bride be grieved when she is wed against her will.
And from that time Daphnis was first among the shepherds,
and, while still in his early youth, he wed the Naiad nymph.

9. The Singing-Match: Daphnis and Menalcas
Daphnis
Sweetly the calf lows, and sweetly the cow,
sweetly the pipe and the cowherd, and sweetly too I sing.
I have a couch of leaves by the cool water, and on it are heaped
the fair hides of white heifers, which all of them
the southwest wind, as they browsed the arbutus, shook down from the crag.
And of the burning summer I take as little heed
as a lover takes of his father's words and his mother's.
So Daphnis sang to me, and so did Menalcas.
Menalcas
Etna, my mother, I too dwell in a fair cave
among the hollow rocks; and I have such things as appear
in a dream: many sheep, and many she-goats,
whose fleeces lie about my head and at my feet.
In a fire of oak the puddings boil, and dry beech-nuts
roast in the fire when it freezes; and I care no more
for winter than a toothless man cares for nuts when porridge is by.
I clapped my hands for them, and at once gave each a gift,
to Daphnis a club, which my father's field reared for me,
self-grown, such as not even a craftsman could fault,
and to the other a fine spiral whelk-shell, whose flesh I myself
had eaten, watching among the Icarian rocks,
cutting it into five for the five of us; and he blew a blast on the shell.
Hail, pastoral Muses, and bring to light the songs
that once, in those herdsmen's company, I sang;
and may I never raise a blister on my tongue's tip again.
Cicada is dear to cicada, and ant to ant,
and hawks to hawks, but to me the Muse and song.
Of these may all my house be full. For neither sleep
nor sudden spring is sweeter, nor to the bees
their flowers; so dear to me are the Muses. Whomever they look upon
they make glad, and those Circe never harmed with her draught.

16. The Graces, or Hiero
This is ever the care of the daughters of Zeus, and ever of singers:
to hymn the immortals, to hymn the glorious deeds of good men.
The Muses are goddesses, and goddesses sing of gods;
but we are mortals here, and let mortals sing of mortals.
For who of all who dwell beneath the gray dawn
will open his door and gladly receive my Graces
when they spread their wings, and not send them off again unrewarded?
But they come back home in anger, on bare feet,
reviling me much because they went a fruitless journey,
and reluctant once more, in the bottom of an empty chest,
they remain, their heads cast down upon their cold knees,
where their seat is always, when they return unsuccessful.
Who of men now is of such a kind? Who will love the one who speaks well of him?
I do not know; for men no longer, as before, are eager
to be praised for noble deeds, but are mastered by gain.
Each, with his hands under his cloak, looks about for where he may get
silver, and would not rub the rust off a coin to give to anyone,
but at once declares: The shin is nearer than the knee;
let me have something for myself; the gods honor singers.
And who would listen to another? Homer is enough for all.
He is the best of singers, who shall take nothing from me.
Foolish men, what gain is the countless gold
lying within? This is not what the wise count the use of wealth,
but to give some to one's own soul, and some to a singer,
and to do good service to many kinsmen, and to many other
men besides, and ever to offer altar-sacrifice to the gods,
and not to be a bad host, but having welcomed a guest at table
to send him off when he wishes to depart,
and above all to honor the holy interpreters of the Muses,
so that even when hidden in Hades you may be heard of as noble,
and not lament without glory by cold Acheron,
like some man with hands callused inside by the mattock,
bewailing the bare poverty he has inherited from his fathers.
Many in the halls of Antiochus and of lord Aleuas
received their monthly measure of food, the bondsmen;
and many calves, driven to the pens of the Scopadae,
lowed along with the horned cattle,
and over the Crannonian plain countless
choice sheep the shepherds folded for the hospitable Creondae;
but no joy of these was theirs, when they had poured out their sweet
life into the wide raft of hateful Acheron,
and, forgotten, leaving behind all those many blessings,
among the wretched dead they lay through long ages,
had not that singer of Ceos, with his varied voice,
set them, named, on the many-stringed lyre among men
of later days; and even the swift horses won honor,
that came back garlanded for them from the holy games.
And who would ever have known the chiefs of the Lycians, who the long-haired
sons of Priam, or Cycnus pale as a woman in his skin,
had not singers hymned the battles of men of old?
Nor would Odysseus, who wandered a hundred and twenty months
among all peoples, and went living to the farthest Hades,
and escaped the cave of the deadly Cyclops,
have had long-lasting fame; and silent would Eumaeus
the swineherd have been, and Philoetius, busy
with the herded cattle, and great-hearted Laertes himself,
had not the songs of the Ionian man profited them.
From the Muses good fame comes to men,
but the living waste the wealth of the dead.
Yet equal is the labor of measuring the waves upon the shore,
as many as the wind drives landward from the gray sea,
or of washing clean a brick of mud with clear water,
and of trying to win over a man corrupted by love of gain.
Farewell to such a man; let him have countless
silver, and let longing for more ever possess him.
But I would choose honor and the friendship of men
before many mules and horses.
I seek to whom of mortals I may come welcome
with the Muses; for hard are the roads for singers
without the daughters of Zeus, who counsels greatly.
Not yet has the sky grown weary of leading round the months and the years;
many horses shall yet turn the chariot-wheel;
there shall be a man who will have need of me as his singer,
having done as great deeds as great Achilles or heavy Ajax
in the plain of Simois, where lies the tomb of Phrygian Ilus.
Already now the Phoenicians who dwell beneath the setting sun
on the farthest verge of Libya are shuddering with dread.
Already the Syracusans grip their spears by the middle,
their arms weighed down with shields of willow;
and among them Hiero, equal to the heroes of old,
girds himself, and horsehair plumes shade his helmet.
Would, O most glorious Zeus, father, and lady Athena,
and the Maiden, who with your mother have for your portion the great city
of the rich Ephyraeans by the waters of Lysimeleia,
that an evil necessity might send our enemies out of the island
over the Sardinian wave, bearing word of the death of dear ones
to children and to wives, few to be counted out of many;
and that the cities might again be dwelt in by their former citizens,
all that the enemies' hands ravaged to the ground;
and that men might work the flourishing fields; and that the countless
thousands of sheep, fattened on the pasture,
might bleat over the plain, and that the cattle, coming in herds
to the steading, might hasten the homing wayfarer at dusk;
and that the fallow lands might be worked toward the sowing, when the cicada,
watching the shepherds at noon, sheltered within the trees,
sings in the boughs; and that the spiders might spread their fine
webs over the armor, and that of the war-cry there might not be even a name.
And may singers carry the high fame of Hiero
both beyond the Scythian sea and to where the broad wall
that Semiramis bound with bitumen reigned over the land.
I am but one, and the daughters of Zeus love many
others too; and may they all care to hymn Sicilian Arethusa
with her peoples, and the spearman Hiero.
O goddesses, daughters of Eteocles, you who love
Minyan Orchomenus, once hateful to Thebes,
unbidden indeed would I stay at home, but to those who call
I would come boldly, with my Muses.
Nor will I leave you behind; for what is dear to men
apart from the Graces? May I be ever with the Graces.
